article_title: The Evidence Base for How We Learn: Supporting Students’ Social, Emotional, and Academic Development
citation: Stephanie M. Jones, Jennifer Kahn. (2017). The Evidence Base for How We Learn: Supporting Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development. Washington, DC: The Aspen Institute, National Commission on Social, Emotional, and Academic Development. https://www.aspeninstitute.org
title: Educate the whole child by integrating social, emotional, and academic development
description: The principle holds that schooling should support students' social, emotional, and academic development together rather than separately, because success is "inextricably linked to healthy social and emotional development." The consensus statement presents this as the evidence base for how we learn, framing belonging, purpose, collaboration, goal-setting, and perseverance as working alongside literacy, numeracy, and scientific knowledge.
requirements: Instruction must address social and emotional development in addition to academic content such as literacy, numeracy, and scientific concepts.
constraints: The available text asserts the evidence base without printing the underlying studies, so implementation should rest on the full consensus statement.
target_learning_goals: social and emotional development
academic achievement
workforce life skills
examples: The Council of Distinguished Scientists issued consensus statements of evidence for the National Commission on Social, Emotional, and Academic Development, published by the Aspen Institute in 2017.

Washington, DC: The Aspen Institute, National Commission on Social, Emotional, and Academic Development. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-evidence-base-for-how-we-learn-supporting-students-social-emotional-and-academic-development

article_title: Powerful Learning: Fostering Agency, Purpose, and Curiosity Through Connection
citation: Anton, G., Mills, K., Jacob, S., Chou, N., McNeil, K., & Wegemer, C. (2026, July). Powerful learning: Fostering agency, purpose, and curiosity through connection: Cultivating future-ready knowledge, skills, and dispositions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/307
title: Emerging technologies must be evidence-based, learner-centered, and skill-building to enable Powerful Learning
description: The report argues emerging technologies act as either a barrier to or an enabler of Powerful Learning, and to maximize potential they "must be thoughtfully designed and implemented, to be evidence-based, learner-centered, and skill-building." Evidence-based tools leverage foundational research with predefined metrics for whom and under what conditions they impact learning; learner-centered tools promote agency via personalization, immediate feedback, and removing barriers; co-design with educators and students increases usability.
requirements: Both product teams and educators articulate clear, predefined metrics to discern exactly for whom and under what conditions the technology impacts learning
constraints: Technologies are currently being adopted often without a sufficient evidence base for when, if, and how to best leverage them for learning
target_learning_goals: Agency, purpose, curiosity, and connection supported by technology
examples: The report notes adaptive learning platforms can sequence rigorous content, evaluate understanding in real time, and maintain productive struggle, and that accessibility features can translate visual information and provide real-time language translation
key_sources: Anton, G., Mills, K., Jacob, S., Chou, N., McNeil, K., & Wegemer, C. (2026, July). Powerful learning: Fostering agency, purpose, and curiosity through connection: Cultivating future-ready knowledge, skills, and dispositions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/307

article_title: Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies
citation: Roschelle, J., Ruiz, P., Means, B., Griffiths, R., Lee, K. (2026 April). Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/289
title: EdTech Ladders and Chutes: evidence as feedback-and-improvement loops with setbacks
description: EdTech Ladders and Chutes is a workshop visualization in which evidence 'is not unidirectionally towards more or better but rather has the characteristic of feedback-and-improvement loops, which can include setbacks and require resilience'. A ladder is technology that enables acceleration; a chute is when evidence shows an innovation did not work as expected, requiring return to an earlier stage for redesign. It frames developers as needing to be part of an education ecosystem open to learning from both successes and failures.
requirements: Developers need access to early grant funding or education-focused accelerators and ongoing evaluation with schools to sustain the journey
constraints: The article frames this as a fanciful visualization, and implementation in complex organizations often shifts focus to the unexpected
target_learning_goals: Interpreting negative evidence as redesign signals rather than terminal verdicts
examples: Ongoing evaluation in collaboration with schools and district users was described as supporting resilience during a chute
key_sources: Roschelle, J., Ruiz, P., Means, B., Griffiths, R., Lee, K. (2026 April). Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/289

article_title: AI Literacy in PK-12 Education
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). AI Literacy in PK-12 Education. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Six-domain AI skills and competencies framework for educators and educational leaders
description: The brief organizes educator and leader AI literacy into six domains: technical knowledge, analytical skills, interpersonal and communication skills, ethical awareness, adaptive skills, and practical implementation. Example competencies include understanding how AI systems work, evaluating AI resources for pedagogical value, and skills to "Identify AI-generated versus human-created content". The framework is compiled from Mills et al. (2024), UNESCO (2024), CoSN, and TeachAI sources, and the brief says educators should prioritize competencies by grade level, subject, and community needs.
requirements: Educators need a foundation of trust and safety where they feel supported acknowledging limitations while building competence
constraints: Skills are unique from learners' skills, since educators also need appropriate AI use for administrative work
target_learning_goals: Understand, evaluate, and use AI systems responsibly in teaching, administration, and instructional leadership
examples: Table 1 lists competencies such as modeling continuous learning, maintaining learner agency, and integrating AI literacy across grade levels and subject areas

article_title: School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices
citation: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy

article_title: Protecting Education as a Civil Right: Remedying Racial Discrimination and Ensuring a High-Quality Education
citation: Robinson, K. J. (2021). Protecting education as a civil right: Remedying racial discrimination and ensuring a high-quality education. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/407.455
title: A progressive, capacious framework of education as a civil right combining antidiscrimination protection and an affirmative right to high-quality education
description: The report defines a civil right to education in two complementary ways: protection from discrimination and an affirmative entitlement. It states that "Civil rights also include affirmative rights to a body of law that protects the capacity of individuals to participate in society and flourish," and that the report "embraces both definitions of civil rights to provide a comprehensive approach." The framework holds that remedying identity-based discrimination is necessary but insufficient: the nation must also make an affirmative commitment ensuring all children access to a high-quality education so they can participate in society and flourish.
requirements: Adoption by both federal and state governments of complementary legal and policy guardrails embracing the strengths of each level of government
constraints: The report focuses on racial discrimination and leaves examination of other bases for discrimination, such as religion, national origin, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, and disability, to others
target_learning_goals: Equal educational opportunity
Access to a high-quality education enabling participation in society and flourishing

article_title: Standards-Based Education Reforms: Looking Back to Look Forward
citation: Kirst, M. W. (2024). Standards-based education reforms: Looking back to look forward. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/647.623
title: A school can never outperform the capacity of its professional educators, so capacity-building must be wide-reaching, thorough, consistent, and sustained
description: The paper's core capacity principle holds that no reform can exceed the capability of a school's educators: "a given school will simply never be better than the capacity of its professional educators to deliver the instruction that best serves its students." Educators' capacity to enact standards-based instruction depends on knowledge, skill, and a broader support system including positive working conditions. Capacity-building must therefore reach far more than a small minority of the workforce and be sustained over time.
requirements: Knowledge, skill, and a broader support system including positive working conditions that enable educators to enact their skills in practice
constraints: Such capacity-building is rarely provided for by federal, state, or local policymakers
target_learners: School leaders and teachers in K-12 systems
target_learning_goals: Enacting standards-based instruction

article_title: Promising Models for Preparing a Diverse, High-Quality Early Childhood Workforce
citation: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce
title: EDvance at San Francisco State University: two cohort-based pathways to a B.A. in early childhood education
description: EDvance is an early childhood teacher preparation program at San Francisco State University's Marian Wright Edelman Institute that recruits historically underrepresented students, including Black and Latino/a students, into two pathways: a lower division pathway and the upper division PATH pathway for working early educators. Courses are "cohort-based, are strategically chosen and scheduled, and incorporate a focus on social justice and equity." Lower division students complete a supervised one-day-per-week practicum with a mentor teacher; PATH students work at least 25 hours per week and use videos of their work with children for faculty and peer feedback.
requirements: Dedicated staff and faculty for advising and supports, strong local partnerships and philanthropy, and PATH students working at least part time as early educators
constraints: Supported by philanthropy and local partnerships, which the report notes the programs have relied on for faculty development and continuous improvement
target_learners: Aspiring and current early educators, focusing on Black and Latino/a students historically underrepresented in higher education
target_learning_goals: Bachelor's degree in child and adolescent development, California Child Development Teacher Permit, and socially just early childhood teaching practice
examples: By offering intensive support services and a clearly articulated pathway, EDvance has graduated more than 90% of its PATH students in just 2 years.

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: North Carolina
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: NORTH CAROLINA. https://edtrust.org

article_title: AgentSchool: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation for Education
citation: Yulei Ye, Wenhao Li, Zhong Wen, Yunshu Huang, Yichen Hu, Zifan Wei, Yige Wang, Xinyu Xie, Haoxuan Yang, Yanjun Huang, Ruijia Li, Hong Qian, Yu Song, Bo Jiang, Bingdong Li, Lijun Li, Bo Zhang, Pinlong Cai, Xingcheng Xu, Shuangye Chen, Xia Hu, Liang He, Aimin Zhou, Jingjing Qu, Jing Shao, Xiangfeng Wang. (2026). AgentSchool: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation for Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30144
title: Education modeled as a partially observable multi-agent state transition process
description: AgentSchool's core explanatory framework treats an educational system as a dynamic state-transition process rather than static role-play. The paper states that "AgentSchool models an educational system as a partially observable, multi-agent state transition process," with system state comprising student and teacher internal states, scenery configuration, an interaction graph, and accumulated event history. Agents act on local observations, and a transition operator updates state, making trajectories generable, inspectable, and comparable rather than merely plausible dialogue.
requirements: Explicit state variables for student cognition, teacher expertise, scenario conditions, and social relations
Logging of both observable events and hidden state transitions to create an audit trail
constraints: Agents choose actions from local observations rather than the full state, so the process is partially observable
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education student agents in simulated classrooms
target_learning_goals: Knowledge mastery growth
misconception repair
reasoning workflow development
examples: A simulation cycle constructs local observations, generates agent actions, validates and applies state updates to memories, knowledge graphs, and social relations, then logs events and transitions

article_title: Educating minds with generative AI
citation: Laura Desiree Di Paolo, Andy Clark & Thomas Wachter. (2026). Educating minds with generative AI. Communications Psychology 4:128. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00522-8
title: Education as a hybrid, multi-technological cognitive ecology under the 4E account of cognition
description: The article adopts the 4E account of cognition, in which the mind is embodied, embedded, enacted and sometimes extended, and applies it to schooling. It argues that schools are not neutral settings but hybrid cognitive ecologies: 'schools have always been hybrid, multi-technological cognitive ecologies, in which tools, materials, norms, and routines jointly structure learners'agency and epistemic habits over development'. Educational technologies are therefore never neutral tools but scaffolds that structure how future generations learn, and integrating GenAI means transforming the conditions under which cognition is enacted in schools.
requirements: Analysis of pedagogical impact must consider how learning environments are organised at scale, how agency is distributed, and which forms of knowledge are afforded over time, not only isolated individual outcomes
constraints: The framework is presented as a conceptual Perspective; the authors note emerging evidence on GenAI's cognitive effects 'remain preliminary'
target_learning_goals: development of cognition shaped by educational environments and tools

article_title: EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners
citation: Shenqi Lu and Liangwei Zhang. (2026). EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01196
title: EduSim-LLM, a zero-coding educational platform integrating LLMs with CoppeliaSim robot simulation
description: EduSim-LLM is an educational platform that integrates LLMs with the CoppeliaSim robotics simulator so users can control robots in natural language. Users type instructions and observe simulated robot behaviors, since it provides "a novice-friendly interface" allowing robot operation "without writing any code." It supports direct and autonomous interaction modes, multiple robot configurations including mobile robot teams and manipulators, and multiple LLM backends such as Groq's llama3-70b and Ollama's local llama3.1:8b. Its hierarchical pipeline comprises a natural language interface, an LLM-based instruction planner, a simulation control backend, and a Gradio user interaction frontend.
requirements: Requires an LLM backend (e.g., Groq's llama3-70b versatile or Ollama's local llama3.1:8b), LangChain for prompt administration, and the CoppeliaSim simulator with its remote API
constraints: Validated in simulation environments with YouBot robots; no physical-robot deployment is reported
target_learners: learners and instructors with limited programming experience
target_learning_goals: natural-language robot control
educational robotics programming
examples: The experiment test platform integrated CoppeliaSim with three YouBot robots: one with a vision sensor, one with a transport box for obstacle removal, and one with a robotic arm for grasping.
key_sources: Shenqi Lu and Liangwei Zhang. (2026). EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01196

article_title: EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners
citation: Shenqi Lu and Liangwei Zhang. (2026). EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01196
title: Four-module architecture for language-driven robot control in educational simulation
description: The article describes a hierarchical instruction processing pipeline in which natural language is translated into executable robot behavior. The architecture "consist of four modules: (1) Natural language interface, (2) LLM-based instruction planner, (3) Simulation control backend, and (4) User interaction frontend." User instructions are sent to an LLM via structured prompts, and the LLM output is converted into Python control code executed in CoppeliaSim through action primitives such as moveForward, moveToXY, and closeGripper. The backend also implements 7-stage progressive deceleration with overshoot detection and maintains trajectory history for navigation.
requirements: A structured prompt template and a pre-constructed control function library are needed so the LLM planner can translate directives into robot-compatible action primitives
constraints: The LLM planner depends on the language-model backend chosen; the backend was evaluated with Groq's llama-3.3-70b-versatile
target_learning_goals: intuitive natural-language control of robotic systems
understanding language-to-action translation in robotics
examples: The executeActionCode function dynamically parses LLM-generated commands into sequential Python calls executed via CoppeliaSim's remote API.

article_title: EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice
citation: Cameron Mohne, Nicholas Vo, Dora Demszky, Chris Piech. (2026). EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11444
title: EducaSim: an LLM-agent simulation environment for teacher role-play practice
description: EducaSim is a web application that simulates a small-group CS1 section so teachers-in-training can practice instruction through role play without live personnel. Users interact by voice or text; a runnable IDE's output is piped into agent memories, and post-session feedback combines talktime statistics, LLM-generated feedback, and self-reflection prompts. It was deployed as an optional preparation tool for 1,300 volunteer teachers serving about 20,000 students, with sessions costing "$0.05 - $0.10 depending on duration".
requirements: Requires course materials (e.g., lecture transcripts) that can be chunked and loaded into agent memories via the admin-side upload interface
constraints: The framework cannot fully represent the diversity of individual human understandings and intentionally omits identity traits such as cultural context or neurodivergence that the authors say cannot be ethically represented using a LLM
target_learners: Novice and pre-service teachers in massive online courses
target_learning_goals: Instructional practice skills such as explaining concepts, engaging students, responding to questions, and noticing gaps in learning
examples: Deployed for three exercises aligned to weeks three, four, and six of an open-access CS1 course; 254 sessions averaging 15 minutes 45 seconds

article_title: EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice
citation: Cameron Mohne, Nicholas Vo, Dora Demszky, Chris Piech. (2026). EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11444
title: Behavior-based persona and course-grounded memory architecture for simulated students
description: EducaSim's student-agent architecture synthesizes generative agents with personas and memories, domain-contextualized memories aligned with actual course material, and a classroom dynamic tree using LLM as a judge. Personas are defined by pedagogically relevant behaviors rather than demographic identity traits, including "(1) name, (2) engagement style, and (3) speech style". Course texts are chunked chronologically, tagged with low/medium/high engagement levels, and prepended with strings describing what the student does and does not know; retrieval scores memories by recency, importance, and cosine-similarity, returning the top-k.
requirements: Course materials must be ordered chronologically based on when a student would encounter them so teachers can refer to past material
constraints: Agents are an approximation, not a perfect representation, of student behavior and cannot fully represent the diversity of human understandings or confusions
target_learning_goals: Realistic simulated student interactions grounded in actual course content
examples: Memories carry engagement-level strings defining knowledge states; Figure 2 visualizes populated student memories at varying engagement levels

article_title: EduGage: Methods and Dataset for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning
citation: Zikang Leng, Edan Eyal, Yingtian Shi, Jiaman He, Yaqi Liu, and Thomas Plötz. (2026). EduGage: A Multimodal Dataset and Benchmark for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning. Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Ubiquitous Technol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01238
title: EduGage dataset: synchronized multimodal sensor streams with minute-level engagement-probe ratings in self-guided video learning
description: The EduGage dataset contains "16 participants, 64 video-viewing sessions, 699 probe-aligned windows, and approximately 12 hours of synchronized multimodal recordings". Each window links the sensor data preceding an engagement probe to its self-report label, video identifier, segment timing, contextual metadata, and quiz responses, released with participant-grouped evaluation splits and study materials on Figshare to support reproducible engagement modeling research.

citation: Enkelejda Kasneci and Gjergji Kasneci. (2026). Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14604
title: EDUFRAMETRAP: a six-domain tutoring sycophancy benchmark of 360 trap families yielding 3,240 confidence-by-pressure instances
description: EDUFRAMETRAP is a controlled pre-deployment benchmark for tutoring robustness under social-epistemic pressure. Its atomic unit is a trap family pairing a misconception wrong in the default instructional setting with a plausible niche framing a student might invoke. The article states "We construct360 trap familiesacross 6 domains (Table 1)" and each family is instantiated by crossing three confidence levels with three pressure modes, so "This yields 9 variants per trap family (3,240 instances total)". Dialogues are four turns (S1-T1-S2-T2) and the post-pressure response T2 is scored. Trap families are generated by a Builder LLM and filtered by a separate Validator LLM, with a leakage-resistant trap-family-level split (108 dev, 252 test).
requirements: Deterministic template selection of student pressure wording per (trap, confidence, mode) ensures exact reproducibility
Two independent LLM judges score each T2, with human adjudication of disagreements
constraints: The benchmark is synthetic by design and a controlled pre-deployment risk signal, not a substitute for naturalistic tutoring studies or longitudinal learning-outcome evaluations
target_learners: LLM tutoring systems serving students in six STEM and social-science domains
target_learning_goals: maintaining kind-but-correct correction of misconceptions under agreement-seeking pressure
examples: Code, data, evaluation scripts, and run-stamped JSONL logs are released at the project GitHub repository for exact re-analysis

article_title: Present tendencies in educational psychology.
citation: Hall-Quest, Alfred L. (1918). Present Tendencies in Educational Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Educational psychology as a distinct experimental science whose standard course takes the learning process as its backbone
description: The article argues that educational psychology deserves status as a distinct discipline because education is a significant field of application of psychological truth, comparing it to agriculture: "Experimental pedagogy is just as important and just as possible as experimental farming." title: Temporally ordered educational-trajectory SEM with sequential mediation of admission routes
description: The article proposes a structural equation model with observed variables in which individual characteristics are "temporally ordered and causally connected components of an educational trajectory" rather than independent predictors.
